Briefly introduce yourself as Muritala, Muyideen Babatunde, a Master of Information Technology candidate in the Department of Computer Sciences, University of Lagos. State the research title clearly. Mention that the work is supervised by Professor C.O. Uwadia and Dr R.A. Koleoso, and that the defence presents a designed, implemented and technically evaluated web-based maternal health monitoring system for the Nigerian healthcare environment.

Explain that Nigerian maternal healthcare still depends on scheduled antenatal visits. Complications can appear between contacts, records are often fragmented, and clinicians cannot easily rank urgency across a large caseload. Digital capture plus guideline-based risk assessment is relevant because it supports continuity, earlier attention and more coherent referral. Do not dwell on mortality statistics. Emphasise the monitoring gap, not a claim that software will reduce deaths.

Present the five operational gaps: continuity, delayed detection, fragmented records, weak automated triage, and weak referral matching. Link each gap to a consequence. Close with the research statement. Do not describe the solution architecture here; that belongs on later slides. The gap is an integrated monitoring, risk-assessment and referral platform suitable for Nigerian antenatal care.

State the aim first: design, implement and deploy a monitoring, risk-assessment and referral system for Nigeria. Then walk the six objectives as a chain: requirements, data store, patient portal, risk engine, clinician dashboard, and location-based referral plus evaluation. Each objective is a necessary part of the artefact, not a separate study.

Summarise three literature clusters: monitoring challenges, digital maternal-health tools, and the integration gap. Use the table to show that existing work often solves one fragment of the problem. Then mention HBM and TAM briefly: HBM informs why women may report symptoms; TAM informs why usefulness and ease of use matter for adoption. The contribution is an integrated artefact, not a new epidemiological study.

Justify Design Science Research: the contribution is a working information-systems artefact, not a survey. DSR’s build–evaluate cycle matches Scrum. Requirements came from WHO, ACOG and NICE guidance plus six antenatal scenarios. Four two-week sprints produced the database, clinical records, decision support and hardening. Evaluation is technical verification on seeded data, not a clinical trial.

Identify the three user roles and what each may do. Patients capture and review their own records. Clinicians see assigned caseloads, alerts and referrals. Administrators manage users and access. Supporting services — the risk engine, notifications, facility matching, assistant and audit controls — sit behind those roles. Mention the non-functional requirements without turning the slide into a full SRS.

Walk the three tiers top to bottom. Stress that the backend is Next.js Route Handlers on Node.js, not a separate Express server. Show the round trip: browser to presentation, to application logic, to Prisma/PostgreSQL, then back. Name Vercel, Neon and Cloudinary as the deployed services. This is the main technical architecture slide — be precise.

Explain that maternal records live in PostgreSQL 16 via Prisma. Sketch the main entity groups rather than every column. Then cover security as a stack: hashing, JWT cookies, RBAC, validation, TLS, role-restricted queries and short-lived reset tokens. Sensitive health data is never treated as a public resource.

Walk the pipeline from data collection to alerts. Emphasise fourteen predictors, weighted scoring, and emergency overrides that can raise the class even when the numeric score is lower. State the LOW / MEDIUM / HIGH thresholds exactly. Stress two safety points: missing vitals are not treated as normal, and the live engine is deterministic TypeScript, not a production Random Forest. The system is decision support, not a diagnostic device.

Demonstrate the journey: a woman registers with her last menstrual period, lands on a dashboard showing gestational age and risk, logs a symptom, sees a classification with contributing factors, and a clinician reviews caseload and alerts. Referral then recommends a suitable facility by location, emergency capability and service need. Present this as a walkthrough of the artefact on seeded data, not a clinical claim.

Report only what was tested: unit, functional, integration and eight clinical scenarios on seeded data. State the four headline counts. Mention the two-second informal observation with its workstation limitation. Explicitly refuse claims of diagnostic accuracy or reduced mortality. If asked about 92.4% accuracy, say that figure is not used as a validated clinical result in this defence.

Frame the contribution as design knowledge: an integrated platform, an explainable engine, and a traceable evaluation path. Do not claim that maternal mortality fell or that the engine is diagnostically accurate. The value is showing that web technology plus guideline-based rules can be assembled, inspected and technically verified as a decision-support artefact.

Be academically honest. The work is a technical demonstration on synthetic records. State the operational stubs — SMS, facility directory, no DHIS2 — without apology or concealment. Then turn each limitation into a future-research recommendation. This slide shows the candidate understands the boundary between software verification and clinical validation.

Conclude confidently: the artefact was designed, implemented and technically evaluated. Restate the three achievements and the feasibility statement. Acknowledge the supervisors and the panel. Invite questions. If asked about clinical impact, return to the limitation that no field trial was conducted.
